Problems & solutions

How do I fit exercise around work, children and a busy life?

Find room for movement in the week you actually have.

By Nutrition.Fitness · 15 September 2026 · 4 min read

The short answer

Fit exercise into the week you actually have by choosing short, suitable sessions, counting useful everyday movement and planning for interruptions. Include travel, changing and childcare when you assess the time commitment. A repeatable starting routine is more useful than an ambitious timetable you cannot follow. Paying for a programme makes sense only if it helps with your specific obstacles.

Start with your calendar, including the bits nobody puts in a fitness advert: commuting, collecting children, caring responsibilities, making dinner and occasionally sitting down. Then choose activity that can live inside that week.

A programme that requires time you do not have is the wrong starting point. It does not become right because somebody tells you to want the results more.

Count the whole appointment

A “30-minute workout” might take an hour and a half once you travel, change, wait for equipment and get home. Alternatively, a home session might take almost exactly the time on the label, provided the space is safe and you do not need to supervise a child simultaneously.

Write down the complete time cost of each option. Be specific about who is covering responsibilities. “I'll fit it in after bedtime” is a possibility; an agreed slot with a fallback is a plan.

OptionWhat to include in the time costQuestion to settle first
Gym sessionTravel, changing, equipment waits and the workoutCan I reliably get there at the planned time?
Home sessionMaking space, setting up and putting equipment awayCan I exercise safely without another task needing my attention?
Walk or wheel outdoorsThe route, weather preparation and accessIs there a practical, safe route near where I already am?
ClassThe fixed start time, journey and booking arrangementsWhat happens if work or childcare changes?

Use the guidelines as a direction, not an entry test

The NHS adult guidelines recommend at least 150 minutes of moderate activity or 75 minutes of vigorous activity weekly, plus strengthening major muscle groups on at least two days. Shorter sessions can contribute. Start at an appropriate level and build up, rather than treating the weekly target as your first-day assignment.

A starting week with room to breathe

Here is an illustrative schedule for someone who can walk comfortably and wants to establish a routine. It is a scheduling example, not an individual exercise prescription or a complete weekly activity target.

  • Monday: a ten-minute walk during a workable break.
  • Tuesday: a suitable 15-minute home strength session during an agreed quiet slot.
  • Thursday: another ten-minute walk.
  • Saturday: a second suitable 15-minute strength session.
  • Sunday: an enjoyable outing, with its length chosen around current ability and family plans.

The two walks total 20 minutes. The strengthening sessions have a separate purpose; do not automatically count all strength time as moderate aerobic activity. The initial aim is to discover which slots hold up. Add activity gradually as it becomes manageable.

Decide the fallback before the interruption

Give each planned session one alternative. If Tuesday's slot disappears, perhaps Thursday morning works instead. If the journey to the gym is the obstacle, a suitable home option could help. If you are unwell or urgently needed elsewhere, the appropriate fallback may be rest and returning to the next planned session.

A missed workout does not create a debt that must be repaid with a punishing double session. This is a timetable for a human household, not an airline compensation policy.

Review after a couple of ordinary weeks. Which slot was easiest? Which depended on luck? Keep the useful appointments and rewrite the unrealistic ones.

What is worth paying for?

Paying may help if you need clear instructions, appropriate session choices or an organised progression. An in-person trainer may be more useful when you need someone to observe technique. A local class may offer the company and fixed appointment you prefer. Free resources may be entirely sufficient if you already know what you want to do.

NUFI's proposed role is programme and meal-planning structure. Compare the programme details with the time you actually have. Before joining any service, check session lengths, equipment requirements, adaptations and what help is genuinely included.

Your next step is to find two plausible appointments in the coming week. If a programme cannot accommodate them, keep looking. You should not need a quieter life before being allowed to start.

Sources and checks

Information checked on 15 September 2026.
